problems.title: Find Customer Referee
problems.notes: WHERE referee_id != 2 silently drops NULL rows because NULL != 2 evaluates to NULL, not TRUE — must add OR referee_id IS NULL; the canonical three-valued-logic trap

problems.title: Article Views I
problems.notes: SELECT DISTINCT author_id WHERE author_id = viewer_id — a same-row self-comparison, not a self-join; candidates overcomplicate this by joining the table to itself unnecessarily

problems.title: Find Users With Valid E-Mails
problems.notes: REGEXP '^[A-Za-z][A-Za-z0-9_.-]*@leetcode\\.com$' — anchor both ends and escape the literal dot, or 'user@leetcodexcom' passes as a false positive

problems.title: Combine Two Tables
problems.notes: LEFT JOIN Person to Address, not INNER JOIN — the whole point is that people with no address row must still appear with NULL city/state

problems.title: Queries Quality and Percentage
problems.notes: AVG(rating / position) then ROUND(...,2) — computing the ratio per-row before aggregating vs SUM(rating)/SUM(position) after are different (and wrong) numbers; read the definition literally

problems.title: Employees Earning More Than Their Managers
problems.notes: self-join Employee e1 JOIN Employee e2 ON e1.managerId = e2.id — the template every hierarchy/self-referencing-table question reuses; alias discipline (e1 vs e2) is the actual skill

problems.title: Rising Temperature
problems.notes: self-join on DATEDIFF(w1.recordDate, w2.recordDate) = 1 rather than id = id-1 — ids aren't guaranteed contiguous/date-ordered, only recordDate is, and that's the hidden failing case

problems.title: Percentage of Users Attended a Contest
problems.notes: ROUND(COUNT(*) * 100.0 / (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM Users), 2) — the *100.0 forces float division; without it, integer division in MySQL truncates every percentage to 0 or 100

problems.title: Employees With Missing Information
problems.notes: FULL OUTER JOIN isn't in MySQL — emulate with a LEFT JOIN ... UNION ... RIGHT JOIN (or two LEFT JOINs unioned), the standard workaround interviewers expect you to know cold

problems.title: Movie Rating
problems.notes: two independent subqueries UNIONed into one result column — resist the urge to force both answers out of a single joined query, they're unrelated aggregations over different grains

problems.title: Not Boring Movies
problems.notes: WHERE id % 2 = 1 AND description != 'boring' ORDER BY rating DESC — straightforward, but 'boring' with different casing in real data would slip past a naive != check

problems.title: Actors and Directors Who Cooperated At Least Three Times
problems.notes: GROUP BY actor_id, director_id HAVING COUNT(*) >= 3 — HAVING filters post-aggregation, WHERE can't reference COUNT(*); the classic WHERE-vs-HAVING interview gotcha

problems.title: Find Followers Count
problems.notes: GROUP BY user_id ORDER BY user_id — the ORDER BY on the grouping key, not the count, is what the spec silently requires and graders check for

problems.title: Project Employees I
problems.notes: JOIN then GROUP BY project_id, AVG(experience_years) with ROUND(...,2) — join before aggregate, never aggregate each table separately and try to combine averages afterward

problems.title: The Number of Employees Which Report to Each Employee
problems.notes: self-join on reports_to = id, GROUP BY manager, ROUND(AVG(age),0) — MySQL's default ROUND uses round-half-away-from-zero, which matters for the .5 average ages in the test data

problems.title: Employees Whose Manager Left the Company
problems.notes: WHERE salary < 30000 AND manager_id NOT IN (SELECT employee_id FROM Employees) — NOT IN against a column that can contain NULL is a landmine elsewhere, but here employee_id is a PK so it's safe; know why

problems.title: Bank Account Summary II
problems.notes: JOIN then GROUP BY account HAVING SUM(amount) > 10000 — computing balance as a running SUM of signed amounts (positive in, negative out) is the reusable ledger pattern behind every 'account balance' question

problems.title: Exchange Seats
problems.notes: CASE WHEN id % 2 = 1 AND id != (SELECT MAX(id) FROM Seat) THEN id+1 WHEN id % 2 = 0 THEN id-1 ELSE id END — the odd-count edge case (last row unswapped) is the part everyone's first draft misses

problems.title: Last Person to Fit in the Bus
problems.notes: SUM(weight) OVER (ORDER BY turn) as a running total, then filter running_total <= 1000 and take the last turn — window functions replace what would otherwise be a self-join on turn <= turn

problems.title: Restaurant Growth
problems.notes: AVG(amount) OVER (ORDER BY visited_on ROWS BETWEEN 6 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW) after collapsing same-day amounts with a daily SUM first — a 7-day moving average needs the explicit ROWS BETWEEN frame, not a plain PARTITION

problems.title: Department Top Three Salaries
problems.notes: DENSE_RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY departmentId ORDER BY salary DESC) <= 3 — must be DENSE_RANK not RANK, since RANK would let a two-way tie for #1 push the real #2 out of the top-3 entirely

problems.title: Tree Node
problems.notes: CASE WHEN p_id IS NULL THEN 'Root' WHEN id NOT IN (SELECT p_id FROM Tree WHERE p_id IS NOT NULL) THEN 'Leaf' ELSE 'Inner' END — solvable with a self-join, but this is also the natural jumping-off point to demonstrate a recursive CTE for computing node depth if the interviewer pushes further

problems.title: List the Products Ordered in a Period
problems.notes: GROUP BY product_id HAVING SUM(unit) >= 100 with the date filter inside the JOIN condition or WHERE — filter to February 2020 before aggregating, not after, or products sold heavily in other months slip in

problems.title: Sales Analysis III
problems.notes: GROUP BY product_id HAVING MIN(sale_date) >= '2019-01-01' AND MAX(sale_date) <= '2019-03-31' — encodes 'only ever sold in Q1' as a min/max range check in one HAVING clause instead of a NOT EXISTS anti-join

problems.title: Consecutive Numbers
problems.notes: three-way self-join on id, id+1, id+2 all matching num (or LAG/LAG(2) OVER), then DISTINCT — the textbook 'appears N times consecutively' shape; generalizes directly to gaps-and-islands

problems.title: Human Traffic of Stadium
problems.notes: the id-minus-ROW_NUMBER() trick: (id - ROW_NUMBER() OVER (ORDER BY id)) is constant within a run of consecutive ids, turning 'find runs of length >= 3' into a GROUP BY on that constant — THE canonical gaps-and-islands solution to memorize

problems.title: Second Highest Salary
problems.notes: SELECT MAX(salary) FROM Employee WHERE salary < (SELECT MAX(salary) FROM Employee) — the MAX-of-a-subquery trick auto-returns NULL when no second value exists, which is exactly the required 'no answer' behavior, no LIMIT/OFFSET edge-casing needed

problems.title: Trips and Users
problems.notes: join Trips to Users twice (once for client_id, once for driver_id) to exclude banned users on either side before computing the daily cancellation rate — the double self-join-via-two-tables is what trips people up, plus remembering to filter the date range before aggregating

problems.title: Managers with at Least 5 Direct Reports
problems.notes: GROUP BY managerId HAVING COUNT(*) >= 5, then join back to Employee to get the manager's name — an IN-subquery against the grouped managerId list is cleaner than a join on the aggregated result

problems.title: User Activity for the Past 30 Days I
problems.notes: WHERE activity_date BETWEEN DATE_SUB('2019-07-27', INTERVAL 29 DAY) AND '2019-07-27' — a 30-day window ending on a fixed date is 29 days back, not 30; the off-by-one in the interval is the actual test
